# How to brainstorm gift ideas for someone impossible to shop for

> **In short:** Describe the person's age, hobbies, and what they already own to an AI assistant, ask for ideas within your budget, and you'll get a short list of thoughtful suggestions in minutes — even for the friend who seems to own everything.

We all have one. The sibling who already has every kitchen gadget. The coworker who collects hobbies like trading cards. The parent who insists they "don't need anything." Staring at a list of generic gift ideas rarely helps — the suggestions feel hollow, and you end up defaulting to a gift card. A short chat with an AI assistant can break that loop. The trick is telling it enough about the person to work with, and asking in a way that pushes past the obvious.

## Before you start
- Any AI assistant you like — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Le Chat, and DeepSeek all handle this well. Free versions are fine.
- A few facts about the person: their age range, what they spend time on, and things you know they already own.
- About 10–15 minutes total. The longer the chat, the better the suggestions get.

## Step 1 — Gather what you already know about them
Open any notes app — Notes on iPhone, Google Keep, a piece of paper, or even the same chat you'll use with the AI. Spend two or three minutes writing quick facts: their age range, where they live, what they do for work or in retirement, hobbies they talk about, and items you know they already own. Don't aim for thorough — rough notes are enough. If you can't think of facts, write down what they mention most often.
💬 Example: "Dad, 71, lives alone, retired electrician, fixes anything around the house, has a full workshop, plays chess online, drinks black coffee, no pets."
You'll know it worked when you have a few rough lines you can paste into a chat, or simply hold in your head for the next step.

## Step 2 — Open your AI assistant and describe the person
Open your chosen assistant in a browser or app. Look for the chat box near the bottom of the screen — usually a rounded text field with a send arrow on the right. Tap inside and type, or paste, a short description of the person. The clearer your description, the more tailored the gift ideas will be, so include age, what they enjoy, and what they already own. If you can't see a text box, look for a button labeled "New chat" or a pencil icon.
💬 Example: "I need gift ideas for my dad. He's 71, a retired electrician who fixes everything himself, plays online chess with his brother, and already owns a full workshop and most common tools. Budget is around $50. He says he doesn't want anything."
If your assistant has a microphone icon, you can speak the description instead of typing — your words appear as text on the screen. You'll know it worked when the assistant replies with a list of suggestions within a few seconds.

## Step 3 — Add your budget and the things they already own
Look at the reply and send a second message in the same chat, right below the first answer. This time, give two extra pieces of information: a clear budget (write it in plain language, like "around $50" or "under $30"), and a short list of things they already have or hobbies they already do, so the assistant doesn't repeat those suggestions. If you wrote notes in Step 1, paste them in now.
💬 Example: "He already has every screwdriver set, a multitool, and a fancy chess clock. Coffee gear he owns too — French press, espresso machine, the works. Please skip kitchen tools and basic hardware. Keep it under $50."
You'll know it worked when the next set of ideas feels noticeably sharper — fewer generic suggestions, more options tied to his actual life.

## Step 4 — Push for ideas you wouldn't think of yourself
Stay in the same chat and send a third message asking the assistant to move past the obvious. A short instruction like "give me ideas I probably wouldn't think of on my own" works surprisingly well — assistants tend to default to safe, popular answers, and a nudge like this changes what comes back. You can also ask for unusual categories, like experience gifts or small luxuries. If the chat has a "regenerate" or "try again" button, you can use that instead of typing.
💬 Example: "Give me 5 gift ideas I wouldn't come up with on my own. Surprises or unusual angles are welcome — not the usual mugs or socks. He's mobile and active, so standing or walking activities are fine."
You'll know it worked when at least one or two suggestions make you pause and think, "I never would have thought of that."

## Step 5 — Combine the best ideas into a short shortlist
Read through everything the assistant has suggested and pick the three to five that feel right. Don't pick the most expensive — pick the ones that match what you actually know about the person. If you're torn between two, ask the assistant to compare them in a fourth message, or to suggest a small twist on one of them. This is also where you check the practical side: is the gift perishable, digital, or slow to ship?
💬 Example: "Between a yearly chess magazine subscription and a video course with a grandmaster, which would suit a 71-year-old who plays online a few times a week? He's not very techy, but his son could help set things up."
You'll know it worked when you have a final shortlist you actually feel good about — not a list of items that "could" work, but ones you want to give.

## Step 6 — Add a personal touch before you buy
Send one more message asking the assistant to help you make the gift feel personal. A handwritten card, the inside joke, a short phrase you'll write on the tag — these are what turn a generic gift into one the person remembers. The assistant can draft a short message for the card, or suggest what to write in a small dedication note. Plain text is fine; this doesn't need anything fancy.
💬 Example: "Help me write a short, warm card message for my dad — under 60 words, a little funny, no 'world's best dad' cliché. He taught me how to fix my first bike when I was ten."
You'll know it worked when you have a card message that sounds like you, not like the greeting card aisle.

## Common mistakes
- **Vague descriptions.** Telling the assistant "he's into stuff" gives it nothing to work with, and you'll get a list of generic mugs and socks. Two or three specific facts change the result completely.
- **Forgetting to mention what they already own.** Without that, you'll get suggestions they already have — which is the original problem you were trying to solve.
- **Stopping after the first reply.** The first answer is usually a safe, popular list. The fourth or fifth message — where you push for unusual ideas and narrow it down — is where the real gems appear.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the next birthday, holiday, or "just because" moment takes ten minutes instead of an hour of scrolling. You walk in with a real idea, not a last-minute gift card.
- **For your business or work:** the same prompt format — name, context, budget, things to skip — works for client gifts, coworker thank-yous, or small team celebrations. Same idea, different person.
- **If you're just getting started:** try it once for the next occasion on your calendar. You'll see quickly whether it clicks for you, and you can adjust how much detail you give next time.

## Try it now
Pick one person on your gift list, open your favorite AI assistant, and send the first message right now. You can use the example from Step 2 as a template — just swap in their age, what they enjoy, and what they already own.
